proposal.comment: [Playbook] We need Garman to defend and indemnify us and our affiliates against third-party claims (IP infringement, Garman's breach of law, Garman-caused data breach, gross negligence or wilful misconduct), with the usual notice, control and cooperation mechanics; the current Section 13 only indemnifies losses from breach of the title warranty. We have also confirmed that any Sparkling indemnity stays limited to our own content and breach of law.

ops.text: Garman shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Sparkling and its affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting Losses, to the extent arising out of (i) an allegation that the Work or the Maintenance Services infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (ii) Garman's breach of applicable law; (iii) any unauthorized access to or disclosure of Sparkling's data caused by Garman; or (iv) Garman's gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Sparkling shall notify Garman in writing of any such claim, Garman shall have control of the defence and settlement of the claim, and Sparkling shall provide reasonable cooperation in that defence. Sparkling's indemnification obligations under this Agreement, if any, are limited to claims arising from content provided by Sparkling and Sparkling's breach of applicable law.

proposal.summary: Add express Garman defence/indemnity for third-party IP, breach of law, data breach and wilful misconduct claims, with notice/control/cooperation procedure, and cap any Sparkling indemnity.

quote: Garman agrees to indemnify Sparkling and hold it harmless from any and all losses, damages and expenses including without limitation, court costs, arbitration fees, penalties, fines, amounts paid in settlement of claims and reasonable legal fees and expenses of investigation (collectively the "Losses") which Sparkling or any of its respective officers or directors may incur due to a breach of this warranty.
rationale: Section 13's only indemnity is for Losses arising from breach of Garman's title/rights warranty; there is no express defence obligation, no coverage of third-party infringement claims as such (nor of Garman's breach of law, Garman-caused data breach, or gross negligence/wilful misconduct), and no defence procedure. The injunction remedies in (a)-(c) are procure/modify/replace only, with no refund if none is available, so the clause also falls short of the fallback remedy set. We therefore target the preferred position by inserting a single express Garman defence-and-indemnity paragraph with notice, control and cooperation mechanics, and confirming that any Sparkling indemnity is limited to Sparkling-provided content and Sparkling's breach of law. We deliberately do not import the fallback's 3x-annual-fees super-cap or Customer modification/combination/specification exclusions, since Section 15 already carves Section 13 out of the liability limitation and the agreement contains no such exclusions - both positions are better for us than the fallback allows.

verification.notes: All ten preferred elements are delivered in a single inserted paragraph: express defend/indemnify/hold-harmless duty to Sparkling and its affiliates, third-party claim trigger, the four required heads (IP allegation as to the Work and Maintenance Services, breach of law, Garman-caused unauthorized access/disclosure, gross negligence/wilful misconduct), and notice/control/cooperation mechanics, plus the narrowing of any Sparkling indemnity to Sparkling-provided content and Sparkling's breach of law. The preferred level is therefore position-complete. The fallback level is not complete (no refund backstop where procure/modify/replace fails, and no 3x annual fees super-cap), but that is immaterial because completion at either level suffices and the preferred level is met. The missing super-cap is Customer-favourable and should not be added. Minimality holds: the edit is a pure insertion after the existing Section 13 remedies with no deletion or paraphrase of retained language, no survival tail, no at-own-expense or extra damages categories, and it reuses the already-defined term "Losses" rather than importing a new damages formula. The retained ten-day notice and (a)-(c) injunction remedies are favourable existing language and are preserved. Intent is preserved: the new notice mechanic is scoped to "any such claim" under the new paragraph and does not contradict the retained ten-day notice for title-warranty claims; Section 15's carve-out for Section 13 continues to operate on the enlarged indemnity without creating a dangling reference or contradictory retained sentence. Drafting note only (not a defect): control of "the defence and settlement" is given to Garman without a consent qualifier for settlements imposing non-monetary obligations on Sparkling — the checklist only requires that control be allocated, so this does not affect completeness, but we would ordinarily add "provided that no settlement imposing liability or admission on Sparkling shall be made without Sparkling's consent" if a further round is available.

No title to the intellectual property in the Work is transferred to Sparkling by this Agreement.
rationale: Garman owns all IP in the Work, expressly including the Improvements and the Schedule "D" Modifications developed for Sparkling, and the only licence back (Section 2) is a non-transferable, location-limited licence to "use" the Software and Documentation, with additional fees payable for other locations and Section 3(c) prohibiting sublicensing. That fails the fallback: our licence to the deliverables is not perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide or royalty-free and carries no right to modify or sublicense for our business. There is also no limit on Garman's use of Sparkling's converted data. We therefore target the fallback (Garman keeps ownership of its software and know-how under Section 13) by broadening the Section 2 grant, conforming the Section 3(c) sublicence restriction, and limiting Garman's use of our data to processing solely to provide the services. We note the licence term remains subject to the Section 17 termination mechanics, which we address under the termination rule rather than duplicating here.

verification.notes: The fallback checklist is complete on the operative text: Section 2 now reads perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free with express use, modify and sublicense rights for Sparkling's business; Section 3(c) is conformed so permitted sublicensing is not separately barred; and a new clause caps Garman's use of Sparkling's data at processing solely to provide the services. Garman's Section 13 ownership of its own software and know-how is left intact, satisfying the generic-tools element. The preferred level is correctly not claimed: ownership of the Work (including the Schedule "D" Modifications) stays with Garman, there is no assignment to Sparkling, and no sentence states that Sparkling retains all rights in its data. Flagging this as a deviation targeted at the fallback is the right call. Minimality holds. Every deletion in Section 2 is load-bearing: "non-transferable" contradicts the sublicense element; "operating at Authorized Locations" and "at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations" contradict worldwide (and the AS400 fragment would be ambiguous if left orphaned); and the additional-fee sentence directly contradicts royalty-free/worldwide, so retaining it would have created a contradictory retained sentence. No survival tail, expense language or extra procedure was added. Intent is preserved: the Fee Schedule, the Authorized Locations definition (still used in the Future Installations clause) and the termination mechanics survive, and the comment correctly defers the term/termination interaction to the termination rule rather than duplicating it here. Recommended (non-blocking) tightening: Section 13 distinguishes "the Work (including any Improvements or Modifications thereto)" from "the Software", so consider adding "(including any Improvements or Modifications thereto)" to the Section 2 subject matter. Without it, a counterparty could argue the upgraded licence reaches only the base Software and Documentation and not the custom Schedule "D" Modifications that the rationale identifies as our deliverable. Two drafting checks before sending: confirm the new data clause lettered "(c)" does not collide with an existing subsection in the Future Installations/Conversions section (renumber if it does), and consider using the agreement's capitalised services/Support term instead of lower-case "services under this Agreement" so the limitation cannot be read narrowly.

quote: (d) Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights and obligations under this Agreement to any third party without the written consent of the other party.
rationale: Section 20(d) is a flat mutual bar on assignment without the other party's written consent, with no successor/M&A carve-out and no reasonableness standard on consent; Section 3(c) separately prohibits Sparkling from assigning the Agreement except as Garman authorizes in writing. That is walk-away territory (blanket prohibition on Customer assignment with no M&A carve-out) and fails every fallback element. There is no change-of-control clause anywhere in the document, so Garman has no termination or re-pricing right on our change of control. We target the fallback: mutual successor assignment on written notice, with consent for other assignments not to be unreasonably withheld, and we conform Section 3(c) so it no longer contradicts the new right.

verification.notes: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative text of revised Section 20(d): mutual successor assignment on written notice, consent for other assignments, reasonableness standard. The finding is correctly targeted at the fallback and the original flat mutual bar was indeed walk-away territory (no M&A carve-out for Customer). Preferred level is incomplete: no affiliate carve-out for Customer, no absolute Customer-consent gate on Vendor assignment (the mutual successor right lets Vendor assign on notice alone), and no bar on assignment to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred the drafter would need to split the clause — e.g. "Customer may assign to an affiliate or to a successor in a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets without consent; Vendor may not assign without Customer's prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld, and in no event to a competitor of Customer." Minimality holds. The Section 3(c) edit is a narrow conforming deletion of only "assign this Agreement or" — necessary because a retained absolute bar on Sparkling assigning without Garman's written authorization would directly contradict the new mutual successor right in 20(d). The rest of 3(c) (transfer, lease, export, sublicence of the Work) is preserved intact, and no survival tails, procedures, or extra requirements were added. Intent is preserved: no undefined terms, no dangling cross-references, and the Work-transfer controls in 3(c), which serve a different purpose from assignment of the Agreement, survive unchanged. No change-of-control mechanic exists to disturb. Note for the record: the conforming 3(c) deletion does relax a Customer-favourable restriction on Vendor's assignment rights. If the team wants to keep that protection, the cleaner fix at preferred level is to restore "not assign this Agreement" in 3(c) and make the 20(d) successor right Customer-only.

quote: Garman hereby grants to Sparkling, for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use: (i) the Software, safely in executable object code format, at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations; and (ii) the Documentation.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no exclusivity, sole-supplier or minimum-requirements obligation on Sparkling, so the rule's preferred position is satisfied. We reviewed the grant (§2), the restrictions on use (§3, which are limited to copying, assignment/sublicensing, reverse engineering and scope-of-use controls and contain no sourcing restriction), maintenance and support (§10, including Software Repair Service, which does not bar third-party maintenance), fees (§11) and the general provisions (§20), and searched for "exclusive", "sole", requirements/procurement and non-compete formulations. The only uses of "exclusive" run in our favour or are unrelated: the licence to us is "non-exclusive" (p0028), the escrow source-code licence to us is "non-exclusive" (p0115), §15 concerns exclusive remedies, and §20(h) provides non-exclusive jurisdiction. §19 is a mutual employee non-solicit, not an exclusive-dealing covenant. No redline is required and the fallback narrowing mechanics (defined category, 12-month cap, service-level and delivery-date exits) are unnecessary because there is nothing to narrow.

quote: (b) Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman. If Sparkling terminates this Agreement pursuant to this Section 17(b), Sparkling shall cease using the Software at the end of the ninety (90) day notice period, and shall certify to Garman within thirty (30) calendar days of termination that Sparkling has destroyed or has returned to Garman all Software, Documentation and Codes.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no liquidated damages, penalty, minimum-fee or early-termination charge on Sparkling, so it sits at our preferred position. Section 11 obliges Sparkling only to pay the fees set out in the Fee Schedule (p0084); Sparkling's convenience termination right on 90 days' notice (Section 17(b), p0118) carries no exit fee or accelerated fees, and termination for Garman's default converts the licence to perpetual with no further fees plus a refund of prepaid fees for services not rendered (p0128). Section 8 likewise requires Garman, not Sparkling, to repay amounts on rejection. The only monetary exposure identified for Sparkling is chargeable repair services at Fee Schedule rates for Sparkling-caused faults (p0077), which is a service charge rather than a liquidated amount or penalty. No redline required.

quote: Garman hereby grants to Sparkling, for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use: (i) the Software, safely in executable object code format, at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations; and (ii) the Documentation.
rationale: Affiliate coverage is already built into the grant (affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, with no notice condition), and the licence is perpetual while fees are paid, so it is not revocable at will. However, the licence is expressly "non-transferable", Section 3(c) prohibits any transfer of the Work absent Garman's written authorization, and Section 20(d) requires consent for assignment of rights; there is therefore no path to carry the licence to a successor in a merger or acquisition. That fails the fallback element on a material term, so we have made the shortest change at fallback level: a successor transfer right in the grant without Garman's approval, with Section 3(c) conformed so no contradictory prohibition is retained. We have not touched the mutual assignment clause in Section 20(d), which we do not wish to loosen in Garman's favour.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: affiliate coverage was already unconditional in the grant, and the inserted sentence supplies an express M&A successor transfer right exercisable without Garman's approval. Preferred level is not complete: no contractor extension, no express "irrevocable" wording, and no perpetual-term language for a paid-up licence in the operative text; the subscription-termination element cannot be resolved from the supplied clauses. Minimality holds. Three surgical touches — deletion of the contradictory "non-transferable" modifier, one sentence adding the successor right, and a conforming carve-out in Section 3(c) which would otherwise prohibit transferring the Work to any Person. Nothing outside the transferability element was altered; "non-exclusive", the Authorized Locations limit and the additional-fee mechanic all survive, and no survival tail, expense or procedural boilerplate was added. Intent is preserved: the mutual assignment clause in Section 20(d) was deliberately left untouched, so no new Vendor-side assignment exception was created. The direct "without Garman's approval" permission in the grant is the sanctioned route over a broad notwithstanding override; Section 20(d) is the general clause and the grant sentence the specific permission. Repair before sending (drafting hygiene, not a checklist failure): confirm that the grant paragraph is in fact Section 2 before relying on the cross-reference "except as permitted by Section 2" in Section 3(c) — if the grant sits in another numbered section, the carve-out becomes a dangling reference and the Section 3(c) prohibition would revive against the successor transfer. Consider "except as permitted by the licence grant in Section [X]" once verified. If you want to reach the preferred level in a later round, the specific additions required are: (i) "and contractors acting on Sparkling's behalf" in the grant's beneficiary list, (ii) an express "perpetual and irrevocable upon payment of the licence fees" term, and (iii) if any part of the licence is subscription-based, a statement that it may be terminated only for material breach that remains uncured after notice.

mappings.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
The cap is based on 12 months of fees.
Indemnification obligations are uncapped.
mappings.quote: The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14.

mappings.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
mappings.quote: The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14.

mappings.element: Gross negligence is uncapped.
Wilful misconduct is uncapped.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 15 excludes indirect damages but sets no monetary cap, so our direct-damages exposure is unlimited; we add a mutual cap at the fallback position of 12 months' fees. Gross negligence and wilful misconduct sit outside the cap, and the existing carve-out for breaches of Sections 13 and 14 keeps the indemnity and confidentiality obligations uncapped.

ops.text: Each party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the fees paid or payable by Sparkling under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim, and this cap shall not apply to a party's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

proposal.summary: Add a mutual 12-months'-fees aggregate liability cap in Section 15, with gross negligence and wilful misconduct outside the cap.

quote: The exclusive remedy of either party in a claim against the other under this Agreement shall be the recovery of its direct damages.
rationale: Section 15 is the only limitation-of-liability provision; it mutually excludes special, indirect and consequential damages and mutually carves breaches of Section 13 (IP indemnity, p0090) and Section 14 (Confidentiality, p0095) out of the limitation, but it contains no aggregate monetary cap at all, so each party's direct-damages exposure (including ours) is unlimited. That fails the fallback requirement of a mutual cap based on 12 months' fees. We therefore add a single mutual cap sentence inside Section 15 at the fallback level (fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim) with gross negligence and wilful misconduct outside the cap; the existing final sentence of Section 15 keeps the indemnity and confidentiality obligations uncapped, so no further carve-outs are needed. We have not pursued the preferred USD 1,000,000 floor or the additional preferred carve-outs.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

checks.name: cap references 12 months of fees or a fixed floor
no unlimited Customer liability language remains

elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Inserted sentence: "Each party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the fees paid or payable by Sparkling..." — "Each party's" makes the cap bilateral, and no retained sentence states either party's liability is unlimited.

elements.element: The cap is the greater of fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim and USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: The inserted cap is only "the fees paid or payable by Sparkling under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim"; there is no "greater of ... and USD 1,000,000" floor. To reach preferred, the sentence must read "the greater of (a) the fees paid or payable ... and (b) USD 1,000,000".

elements.element: The exclusion of indirect and consequential damages applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Retained Section 15: "In no event shall either party be liable to the other for the recovery of any special, indirect or consequential damages ... including but not limited to lost profits, lost revenues ... loss of data and loss of use."

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Retained section-wide carve-out: "The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14." Section 14 is the Confidentiality provision (p0095). Because the carve-out is drafted against "this Section 15" (not "this paragraph"), it reaches the newly inserted cap sentence as well.

elements.element: Breach of data protection and security obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: No data protection or security carve-out exists; the only carve-outs are Sections 13 and 14 (IP warranty/indemnity and Confidentiality) plus the new gross negligence / wilful misconduct wording. Confidentiality is not a substitute for data protection and security obligations.

elements.element: Indemnification obligations are uncapped.
elements.evidence: "The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14"; Section 13 (p0090) contains Garman's warranty and its indemnity of Sparkling for Losses, so indemnity liability sits outside the new cap.

elements.element: Gross negligence is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "...and this cap shall not apply to a party's gross negligence or wilful misconduct."

elements.element: Wilful misconduct is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "...this cap shall not apply to a party's gross negligence or wilful misconduct."

elements.element: Fraud is uncapped.
elements.evidence: The inserted carve-out names only gross negligence and wilful misconduct; the word "fraud" appears nowhere in Section 15 or the carve-out to Sections 13 and 14.

elements.element: Infringement of the other party's intellectual property is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Section 13 is Garman's warranty that it owns the rights granted plus an indemnity for third-party infringement claims against Sparkling; it is not a mutual carve-out for a party's infringement of the other party's IP. No such carve-out was added.

elements.element: Customer payment obligations are excluded from damages subject to the cap.
elements.evidence: The new mutual cap applies to "total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement" with no statement that Sparkling's obligation to pay fees is not "damages" subject to the cap.

elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: "Each party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed..." — bilateral by its terms; the measurement basis (fees paid by Sparkling) does not make the cap one-sided.

elements.element: The cap is based on 12 months of fees.
elements.evidence: "...the fees paid or payable by Sparkling under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim." Twelve months of fees, at or above the 6-month walk-away floor; "Fees" is not a narrow defined term here, so the cap is not illusory.

elements.element: Indemnification obligations are uncapped.
elements.evidence: Retained final sentence excludes "breaches of Sections 13 and 14" from "the limitation of liability in this Section 15", and Section 13 houses the indemnity obligation (p0090). The reference is section-wide, so it captures the newly added cap sentence.

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Same section-wide carve-out reaches Section 14 (Confidentiality, p0095), which remains outside the new cap.

elements.element: Gross negligence is uncapped.
elements.evidence: "...this cap shall not apply to a party's gross negligence or wilful misconduct."

elements.element: Wilful misconduct is uncapped.
elements.evidence: "...this cap shall not apply to a party's gross negligence or wilful misconduct."

verification.notes: Fallback is complete: the single inserted sentence supplies a bilateral cap at 12 months' fees paid or payable and puts gross negligence and wilful misconduct outside it, while the retained sentence "The limitation of liability in this Section 15 shall not apply to breaches of Sections 13 and 14" keeps the indemnity (s.13) and confidentiality (s.14) obligations uncapped. Because that carve-out is drafted against the whole of Section 15 rather than a single paragraph, it operates on the new cap notwithstanding that the cap sentence is placed after it. Preferred is not complete: no USD 1,000,000 floor ("greater of"), and no carve-outs for data protection/security obligations, fraud, or a party's infringement of the other party's IP; Section 13 covers Vendor's third-party infringement indemnity, not mutual infringement of the counterparty's IP. There is also no statement that Sparkling's payment obligations are not "damages" for cap purposes — with the cap drafted as "total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement", a Vendor could argue our fee obligation is capped, so if the preferred level is pursued, add both the USD 1,000,000 floor and an express payment-obligation exclusion. Minimality holds: one concise sentence added, nothing deleted, no survival tail, no procedure, no extra damages categories, no additional carve-outs beyond the two the fallback checklist requires, and the preferred-only USD 1,000,000 floor was correctly omitted rather than over-asking. Intent is preserved: the exclusive-remedy/direct-damages sentence, the mutual indirect-damages exclusion, the risk-allocation recital and the Sections 13/14 carve-out all survive without contradiction; no defined term, cross-reference or commercial mechanic is left dangling. Optional polish for the same word count: drafting the new sentence as "Subject to the final sentence of this Section 15, each party's total aggregate liability..." would remove any argument that a later-placed cap sits outside the earlier carve-out. Not required for the fallback to be met, but it eliminates the only reading risk in the insertion.

mappings.element: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction.
mappings.quote: a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use

quote: Garman hereby grants to Sparkling, for the use of Sparkling and affiliated companies of Sparkling operating at Authorized Locations, a non-transferable and non-exclusive licence to use: (i) the Software, safely in executable object code format, at each AS400 at each of the Authorized Locations; and (ii) the Documentation.
rationale: The agreement imposes no non-compete or field-of-use restraint on Sparkling. Section 3 (Restrictions on Use) and the related paragraph (g) contain only ordinary licence-scope limits (no copying beyond backups, no reverse engineering, no sublicence/transfer, no service-bureau use of the Work), none of which restrict the businesses Sparkling may operate or the products it may buy or build; Sparkling remains free to acquire or develop competing routing software. Section 19 is a mutual employee non-solicitation, not a non-compete, and is addressed under the non-solicitation rule rather than here. The licence itself is expressly non-exclusive, and no exclusivity, territory, or competing-product covenant appears in the general matters clause or elsewhere. This meets the preferred position, so no redline is proposed.

verification.notes: No proposal: element-level redline verification is not applicable.

quote: (b) Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman.
rationale: Section 17(b) gives Sparkling an unconditional right to terminate the Agreement at any time on ninety (90) calendar days' written notice, which sits squarely at the fallback notice window of 60–90 days. No early-termination fee, penalty or accelerated-payment mechanic attaches to that exit: Section 11 and the Fee Schedule reference only fees payable in the ordinary course, so the fallback cap of three months' fees is satisfied (in fact exceeded, at nil). On the Vendor side, Garman's only termination rights arise under Section 17(c) for insolvency events or an uncured material default; nothing anywhere in the document (including Sections 7, 8 and 10) gives Garman any right to terminate for convenience, so the fallback limits on Vendor convenience termination (end-of-term only, 90 days' notice) are met and the preferred element that Garman have no convenience right during a committed term is also satisfied. Falling short of the preferred position only in that notice is 90 rather than 30 days and there is no express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees on a Sparkling convenience termination (a refund is provided only on Garman default under Section 17(c)); these are noted rather than redlined because the clause meets the fallback on its material terms. This sits at the fallback and we do not propose changes.

verification.notes: No proposal: element-level redline verification is not applicable.

quote: (e) not use the Work except as authorized herein;
rationale: There is no audit, inspection, verification or usage-monitoring right binding Sparkling anywhere in the Agreement. Section 3 (Restrictions on Use, p0030–p0039) imposes copy/use/service-bureau restrictions but gives Garman no right to verify or inspect compliance; Section 10 (Maintenance and Support) provides only telephone/repair services; Section 14 merely defines Confidential Information as including "accounting records for which access is obtained ... pursuant to this Agreement" without granting any access or audit right; and Section 20 (General Matters) contains no inspection or records provision. Because no audit right binds us, the position is better than the preferred checklist (no frequency, notice, cost or system-access risk arises), so no redline is warranted — proposing audit parameters would create a Vendor audit right that does not currently exist and would weaken our position.

verification.notes: No proposal: element-level redline verification is not applicable.

mappings.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We require New York law with exclusive jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County, so we have replaced the Nova Scotia law and non-exclusive Nova Scotia venue in Section 20(h), retaining only a customary carve-out for temporary injunctive relief. Delaware, California, or England and Wales law with the corresponding courts (London for English law) would be an acceptable fallback.

ops.newText: This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of New York. All disputes under this Agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, except that either party may seek temporary injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction.
ops.oldText: This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia. All disputes under this Agreement shall be subject to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Nova Scotia.

proposal.summary: Replace Nova Scotia law/non-exclusive Nova Scotia venue with New York law and exclusive New York County courts

quote: (h) This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Nova Scotia and the laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia. All disputes under this Agreement shall be subject to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Nova Scotia.
rationale: Section 20(h) is the only governing-law/venue provision in the Agreement (no arbitration clause appears anywhere). It selects the laws of Nova Scotia and Canada with non-exclusive Nova Scotia venue. Nova Scotia is not on the accepted list (New York, Delaware, California, England and Wales), so the clause fails both the preferred and the fallback positions on the governing law and on the forum, and the non-exclusive venue leaves no certain merits forum. We therefore propose the preferred target: New York law with exclusive jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County, subject only to a carve-out for temporary injunctive relief. Delaware, California, or England and Wales law with the corresponding courts remains an acceptable fallback.

checks.name: governing law within the accepted set

elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Rendered 20(h): "This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of New York." The Nova Scotia/Canada choice of law is fully displaced.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.
elements.evidence: Rendered 20(h): "All disputes ... shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, except that either party may seek temporary injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction." The carve-out is limited to temporary injunctive relief, so the exclusive merits forum survives.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause selects New York law, not Delaware, California, or England and Wales. This is expected because the drafter targeted the preferred level; the fallback checklist is simply not the level pursued.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: Forum is the state and federal courts in New York County, not Delaware/California courts or the courts of London. Again a consequence of targeting the preferred level.

verification.notes: Position-complete at the preferred level: both preferred elements are satisfied in operative language (New York governing law; exclusive state and federal courts in New York County with a carve-out confined to temporary injunctive relief). The finding is correctly classified as a deviation: the original clause chose Nova Scotia law and non-exclusive Nova Scotia venue, which is outside the accepted set (New York, Delaware, California, England and Wales) and therefore fails both preferred and fallback on governing law and forum. No arbitration clause exists, so no seat issue arises. Minimal: the edit changes only the jurisdiction words and the forum designation, converting non-exclusive to exclusive as the preferred element requires, and adds only the customary temporary-injunctive-relief carve-out that the element itself contemplates. Deletion of the redundant "laws of Canada applicable in Nova Scotia" phrase is part of the same choice-of-law selection, not an extraneous removal. No survival tails, fee-shifting, service-of-process, jury-waiver, or other boilerplate extras were added. Preserves intent: the two-sentence structure, the scope phrase "All disputes under this Agreement," and the surrounding Section 20 boilerplate are retained; no undefined term, dangling cross-reference, or contradictory retained sentence results, and no other allocation, timing, or remedy mechanic is disturbed. Margin comment is compliant with tone: concise, first person plural, states what changed and why, cites the playbook position, and offers the Delaware/California/England and Wales fallback without lecturing. Fallback elements are marked not_met only because the preferred level was targeted; this does not affect position-completeness, which requires completion at either level.

mappings.element: Commercial general liability coverage is at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no insurance covenant even though Garman personnel attend our Authorized Locations and handle our data, so we have added a standard insurance paragraph at § 20(k) (CGL USD 1M/2M, E&O USD 2M, cyber USD 5M where our data is processed, statutory workers' compensation, certificates on request). We can fall back to E&O USD 1M and cyber USD 2M if the full programme is an issue.

ops.text: (k) Garman shall maintain commercial general liability insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate; professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000; where Garman processes any data belonging to, supplied by, or processed for Sparkling, cyber and privacy liability insurance of not less than USD 5,000,000; and workers' compensation insurance as required by law. Garman shall provide certificates of insurance on request.

quote: (j) This Agreement constitutes the entire Agreement between the parties with respect to its subject matter, and this Agreement supersedes all prior understandings, representations, negotiations and communications between the parties, oral and written.
rationale: No insurance covenant exists anywhere in the Agreement: searches for "insurance", "coverage", "certificate" and "workers' compensation" return nothing, and § 20 (General Matters, subsections (a)-(j)) ends with the entire-agreement clause. Garman personnel attend Authorized Locations for installation, data conversion and training and handle Sparkling data, so an uninsured vendor is walk-away territory under the rule. We insert a short § 20(k) at the preferred level (CGL USD 1M per occurrence / USD 2M aggregate, E&O USD 2M, cyber/privacy USD 5M where Sparkling data is processed, statutory workers' compensation, certificates on request), omitting ancillary expense and survival language not required by the checklist.

elements.element: Commercial general liability coverage is at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k): "commercial general liability insurance of not less than USD 1,000,000 per occurrence".

elements.element: Commercial general liability coverage is at least USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k): "and USD 2,000,000 in the aggregate" for the CGL policy.

elements.element: Professional errors and omissions coverage is at least USD 2,000,000.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k): "professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000".

elements.element: If Vendor processes Customer Data, cyber and privacy coverage is at least USD 5,000,000.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k): "where Garman processes any data belonging to, supplied by, or processed for Sparkling, cyber and privacy liability insurance of not less than USD 5,000,000" — the trigger captures every category of Customer data, not selected named types.

elements.element: Vendor maintains workers' compensation coverage as required by law.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k): "and workers' compensation insurance as required by law".

elements.element: Vendor provides certificates of insurance on request.
elements.evidence: New § 20(k) final sentence: "Garman shall provide certificates of insurance on request."

elements.element: Professional errors and omissions coverage is at least USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: E&O is set at USD 2,000,000, which exceeds the USD 1,000,000 fallback floor.

elements.element: Cyber and privacy coverage is at least USD 2,000,000.
elements.evidence: Cyber/privacy is set at USD 5,000,000 where Garman processes any Sparkling data; since Garman handles Sparkling data, the trigger applies and the amount exceeds the USD 2,000,000 floor.

verification.notes: The inserted § 20(k) is a clean, self-contained insurance covenant that renders every preferred element in operative language: CGL 1M/2M, E&O 2M, cyber/privacy 5M on a Customer-Data trigger, statutory workers' compensation, and certificates on request. Minimality holds: the drafter omitted the model language's "at its own expense" and the one-year survival tail, added no notice, additional-insured, waiver-of-subrogation, rating or procedural extras, and left § 20(j) and all other text untouched. Adding new lettered subsection (k) after (j) creates no dangling cross-reference and contradicts no retained sentence. The cyber trigger is drafted as "any data belonging to, supplied by, or processed for Sparkling," which covers every category of Customer data rather than selected named types, so the conditional element is properly satisfied rather than narrowed. Because the clause is genuinely absent from the Agreement (no insurance, coverage, certificate or workers' compensation language anywhere, and § 20 closes with the entire-agreement clause), an insertion is the correct remedy and all-new wording does not defeat minimality. Both levels are complete; no repair is required. The fallback offered in the margin comment is correctly held back for negotiation rather than being drafted into the operative text.

mappings.element: Customer has no most-favoured-nation obligation benefiting Vendor.
mappings.quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: The agreement contains no most-favoured-nation mechanic in either direction. Section 11 (Fees) states Sparkling's entire pricing obligation as payment of the amounts set out in the Fee Schedule, with no obligation to extend Garman terms no less favourable than those given to any third party, and no obligation to disclose or match third-party offers. Searches across the fees, maintenance (Section 10, including the Software Repair Service rate provisions), term/termination and general-matters provisions, and the definitions and schedule list, returned no "most favoured", "no less favourable", best-pricing, comparison, or price-matching language. This satisfies the preferred position (no MFN obligation on Customer), so no redline is warranted; the fallback (defined product, 12-month cap, like-for-like carve-outs) is not engaged because there is no Customer MFN to limit.

verification.notes: No proposal: element-level redline verification is not applicable.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no minimum purchase or volume commitment on Sparkling and no take-or-pay or shortfall mechanic. Searches for "minimum", "commit", "shortfall", "volume", "purchase" and "take or pay" return nothing, and every payment obligation is scoped to what is licensed or ordered: § 11 requires payment only of "the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule"; § 2 charges additional fees only if Sparkling elects to use the Software at locations beyond the Authorized Locations; § 10 maintenance runs on a "renewable one-year term" with no multi-year lock-in; and § 17(a)/(b) keep the licence in effect only "as long as fees are paid" while letting Sparkling terminate at any time on 90 days' notice. Section 3 restrictions are use/copy limits, not volume caps on consumption. This sits at the preferred position (no minimum commitment; fees for ordered services only), so no redline is warranted; we would only revisit if Schedule "A" itself introduced committed licence counts or committed maintenance years.
ruleTitle: Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions on Customer

mappings.element: The non-solicitation restriction is mutual.
The restriction covers only personnel directly involved in the Services.
The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months after the person's involvement ends.
General advertisements are excluded from the restriction.
Unsolicited approaches are excluded from the restriction.
The restriction does not prohibit hiring.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept a no-hire covering all of the other party's employees, so we have narrowed Section 19 to our fallback: a mutual non-solicitation limited to personnel directly involved in the services, running 12 months from the end of that involvement, with carve-outs for general advertisements and unsolicited approaches and no restriction on hiring.

ops.newText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of twelve (12) months after a person's involvement in the provision of services under this Agreement ends, both parties agree not to solicit for employment any employee of the other party who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement; provided that this Section shall not restrict either party from hiring any person, and shall not apply to general advertisements of employment not specifically targeted at the other party's personnel or to unsolicited approaches by any such person.
ops.oldText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Convert the mutual no-hire into a 12-month non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved in the services, with advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs.

quote: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.
rationale: Section 19 is the only responsive clause (searches for solicit/hire/advertising carve-outs return nothing else). It is a mutual no-hire, not a non-solicit, and it reaches "any employee of the other party" rather than only personnel involved in the services; it also runs one year from termination rather than from the end of a person's involvement and has no general-advertising or unsolicited-approach carve-out. A no-hire covering all personnel is walk-away territory, so this fails the fallback on material terms. We narrowed it to the fallback: mutual non-solicitation of personnel directly involved in the services, 12 months after that involvement ends, with advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs and an express statement that hiring is not prohibited.

elements.element: Customer has no non-solicitation restriction.
elements.evidence: The rendered Section 19 still binds "both parties" — i.e. Customer — with a mutual non-solicitation covering the other party's directly involved personnel for 12 months; the preferred position (no restriction on Customer at all) is not achieved.

elements.element: The non-solicitation restriction is mutual.
elements.evidence: "both parties agree not to solicit for employment any employee of the other party" — obligation runs symmetrically in both directions.

elements.element: The restriction covers only personnel directly involved in the Services.
elements.evidence: Limited to "any employee of the other party who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement"; the original catch-all reach to "any employee of the other party" (and to ex-employees within six months) has been removed.

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months after the person's involvement ends.
elements.evidence: "for a period of twelve (12) months after a person's involvement in the provision of services under this Agreement ends" — the temporal anchor is the end of involvement, not termination, replacing the original "one year thereafter".

elements.element: General advertisements are excluded from the restriction.
elements.evidence: "shall not apply to general advertisements of employment not specifically targeted at the other party's personnel".

elements.element: Unsolicited approaches are excluded from the restriction.
elements.evidence: "or to unsolicited approaches by any such person".

elements.element: The restriction does not prohibit hiring.
elements.evidence: The operative verb is changed from "not to hire" to "not to solicit for employment", and an express proviso states "this Section shall not restrict either party from hiring any person"; the affiliate no-hire extension is deleted with the no-hire itself.

verification.notes: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative language: mutuality, involvement-limited scope, 12-months-from-end-of-involvement duration, general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs, and an express no-prohibition-on-hiring proviso all appear in the rendered clause rather than only in the margin comment. Preferred level is correctly not claimed: Customer remains subject to a mutual non-solicit, so a "deviation" finding resolved at fallback is the right posture given the original was a mutual no-hire over all employees (walk-away). Minimality holds: every edit maps to a selected fallback element — verb change hire→solicit for employment (no-hire element), scope narrowing (involvement element), re-anchored 12-month period (duration element), and the added proviso (carve-out and no-hire elements). Deleting "or allow its respective affiliates to hire" and the six-month former-employee tail is part of removing the no-hire and narrowing scope, not an unrelated extra; no survival tail, expense language, procedures, or boilerplate were added. Intent is preserved: the clause remains a mutual restrictive covenant sitting in Section 19, the term-plus-tail structure survives, and no defined term, cross-reference, or retained sentence is left dangling or contradicted. Deterministic checks (duration ≤12 months, general-solicitation carve-out present, element coverage, minimality gate) were inspected in substance against the rendered text and match; no gate is passing on a mere keyword hit.

quote: For a renewable one-year term commencing upon the Maintenance Commencement Date, subject to payment of maintenance fees in accordance with the Fee Schedule but without additional fees or charges, Garman shall provide the following Maintenance Services:
rationale: The only renewal mechanic is the maintenance term in Section 10 (p0065): a "renewable one-year term" of maintenance. There is no automatic renewal language anywhere in the Agreement (a full-text search for "renew" returns only p0065), so no non-renewal notice window is imposed on Sparkling and there is no automatic multi-year renewal or walk-away trap. The Agreement also contains no renewal price-uplift mechanic — maintenance fees are fixed by reference to the Fee Schedule and Section 10 states maintenance is provided "without additional fees or charges" — so no uncapped increase is authorised. Both fallback elements are conditional on automatic renewal / permitted price increases and are therefore satisfied on the material terms; the renewal term is in any event one year, not multi-year. The surrounding term structure favours us: the licence is perpetual so long as fees are paid (p0117) and Sparkling may terminate at any time on 90 days' notice (p0118). Noted short of preferred wording only: the clause does not expressly say renewal is by mutual written agreement, and there is no express CPI/3% cap on any future renewal-period maintenance fee quoted in Schedule "A" (the Schedule is not attached). These are minor sub-elements, not deviations, so we do not redline.

quote: (b) Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman. If Sparkling terminates this Agreement pursuant to this Section 17(b), Sparkling shall cease using the Software at the end of the ninety (90) day notice period, and shall certify to Garman within thirty (30) calendar days of termination that Sparkling has destroyed or has returned to Garman all Software, Documentation and Codes.
rationale: No exit clause exists anywhere. Section 17 addresses only Sparkling's return/destruction of Garman's Software, Documentation and Codes (p0118) and a fee refund on Garman default (p0128); Section 8 return of Sparkling's Confidential Information applies only if the rejection option is exercised pre-acceptance, not on expiry or termination generally; the escrow clause (Section 16) gives source-code continuity but no transition assistance or data return, and Section 18 survival adds nothing absent an operative exit obligation. We therefore insert a single Section 17(d) at the preferred level: up to six months' transition assistance at then-current rates, return of Sparkling's data in a standard machine-readable format within 30 days of expiry or termination, and certified deletion after that return. Survival is already carried by Section 18's general clause, so no collateral edits are needed.

quote: For the acceptance period and for a period of one year from the Maintenance Commencement Date, and thereafter for as long as the Software is covered by Maintenance Services and is used by Sparkling in accordance with this Agreement, Garman warrants that the Software shall perform in conformance with the Specifications in all material respects.
rationale: Section 12 gives a strong software conformance warranty (one year from the Maintenance Commencement Date, plus the acceptance period and any maintenance-covered period), which exceeds the 90-day fallback floor. However, the fallback fails on two material terms: (i) there is no warranty of any duration covering Garman's services (installation, training, Maintenance Services) — nothing in Sections 4, 5, 9 or 10 warrants performance quality; and (ii) Section 12 states no remedy. The only repair mechanic (Section 10(c), p0077) is a best-efforts maintenance service conditional on paid maintenance, and the only money-back mechanic (Sections 7-8) is confined to the acceptance period, is "in lieu of any other remedy" and terminates the Agreement, so there is no refund remedy for warranty breach. We therefore propose the shortest fallback cure: a 30-day services warranty and an express repair/replace-or-refund remedy for the Section 12 warranties. There is no general warranty disclaimer, so the express warranty is not swallowed.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: the retained one-year Software conformance warranty exceeds the 90-day floor, and the single inserted sentence pair supplies the missing 30-day services warranty plus an express repair/replacement-or-refund remedy tied to the Section 12 warranties. Preferred level is not complete: the services warranty is 30 days rather than 90, and there is no compliance-with-laws warranty and no no-malicious-code warranty. To reach preferred, the drafter would need to change "thirty (30) days" to "ninety (90) days" and add express compliance-with-applicable-laws and no-malicious-code warranties. Minimality holds: nothing outside the checklist was deleted or added — no survival tail, no at-own-expense language, no procedural mechanics; the acceptance-period rejection right in Section 7/8 and the best-efforts maintenance repair mechanic in Section 10(c) are left intact. Intent preserved: the new remedy is expressly scoped to "the warranties in this Section 12", so it does not disturb the acceptance-period "in lieu of any other remedy" rejection right (which addresses acceptance failure, a different trigger) or the fee-bearing Software Repair Services carve-out; no undefined terms or dangling cross-references are created. Note for the drafter: because the acceptance-period option is stated to be "in lieu of any other remedy", consider confirming in negotiation that the new Section 12 remedy governs post-acceptance warranty breach — as drafted the two operate on distinct triggers, so no contradiction arises, but the point is worth flagging.
